questions.stem:
A movable metal rod is placed in the middle of a rectangular metal frame as shown. A uniform magnetic field directed out of the plane of the paper acts perpendicular to the frame.

Which of the following actions could lead to a clockwise current flowing through the frame?
questions.stemText: A movable metal rod is placed in the middle of a rectangular metal frame as shown. A uniform magnetic field directed out of the plane of the paper acts perpendicular to the frame. movable rod frame magnetic field Which of the following actions could lead to a clockwise current flowing through the frame? A Decreasing the magnitude of the magnetic flux density of the field. B Increasing the magnitude of the magnetic flux density of the field. C Sliding the rod to the left while maintaining contact with the frame. D Sliding the rod to the right while maintaining contact with the frame.

options.label: A
options.text: Decreasing the magnitude of the magnetic flux density of the field.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing the magnitude of the magnetic flux density of the field.

options.label: C
options.text: Sliding the rod to the left while maintaining contact with the frame.

options.label: D
options.text: Sliding the rod to the right while maintaining contact with the frame.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish circulation around the full frame from circulation in the two subloops.
questions.misconception: Treating the flux change in one subloop as a change through the whole frame

explanation.body: Sliding the rod induces an e.m.f. across it and produces currents in opposite senses in the two loops. Increasing the magnetic flux density increases the outward flux linkage through the frame. By Lenz’s law the induced field points into the page, so the current around the frame is clockwise.

perOption.A: A decreasing outward flux induces an outward field and an anticlockwise current.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Sliding left produces opposite circulation in the two loops, with clockwise circulation only in the right loop.
perOption.D: Sliding right produces opposite circulation in the two loops, with clockwise circulation only in the left loop.

questions.stem:
A uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T passes through a coil of area 20 $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$. The coil has 15 turns and is tilted an at angle of 30 $^{\mathrm{o}}$ as shown.

What is the magnetic flux linkage of the coil?
questions.stemText: A uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T passes through a coil of area 20 cm2. The coil has 15 turns and is tilted an at angle of 30 o as shown. What is the magnetic flux linkage of the coil? A 1.3 × $10^{-4}$ Wb B 7.5 × $10^{-3}$ Wb C 1.3 × $10^{-2}$ Wb D 1.3 Wb

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires the angle to the coil normal and a square-unit conversion.
questions.misconception: Using the coil plane in the cosine formula

explanation.body: The coil normal is at $30^\circ$ to the field. With $A=20\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, the flux linkage is $N\Phi=NBA\cos30^\circ=15(0.50)(20\times10^{-4})\cos30^\circ=1.3\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

perOption.A: Makes the converted area a factor of 100 too small.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin30^\circ$ even though $30^\circ$ is the angle to the coil normal.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Converts the area with a factor of $10^{-2}$ instead of $10^{-4}$.

questions.stemText:
The figure below shows a conducting rod of length $L$ and mass $m$ placed on a very long and smooth plane of width $w$ which makes an angle of $\theta$ to the horizontal. The rod is connected to a resistor of resistance $R$ through light and flexible wires. The rod is then released from rest at the top of the plane and moves in a uniform magnetic flux density $B$ that is vertically downwards everywhere. The rod attains terminal velocity after some time.

[The conducting rod lies across the inclined plane, perpendicular to the downhill direction. Both ends are connected by flexible wires to an external resistor labelled $R$. The plane’s cross-slope width is labelled $w$ and the angle between the plane and the horizontal is labelled $\theta$.]

What is the magnitude of the rod’s terminal velocity?

A $\frac{mgR\tan\theta}{B^2w^2}$
B $\frac{mgR\tan\theta}{B^2L^2}$
C $\frac{mgR\tan\theta}{B^2w^2\cos\theta}$
D $\frac{mgR\tan\theta}{B^2L^2\cos\theta}$

stemImage.alt: Question 25: The figure below shows a conducting rod of length L and mass m placed on a very long and smooth plane of width w which makes an angle of θ to the horizontal. Th

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine motional e.m.f., current and magnetic force, resolving components for both induction and force balance.
questions.misconception: Applying the inclination factor only once

explanation.body: At speed $v$ down the slope, the induced e.m.f. is $BLv\cos\theta$, so $I=BLv\cos\theta/R$. The magnetic force has magnitude $BIL$ and its component up the slope is $BIL\cos\theta$. At terminal speed, $mg\sin\theta=B(BLv\cos\theta/R)L\cos\theta$. Solving gives $v=\frac{mgR\tan\theta}{B^2L^2\cos\theta}$.

perOption.A: Uses the plane width and loses one factor of $\cos\theta$.
perOption.B: Uses the rod length but loses one factor of $\cos\theta$.
perOption.C: Uses the plane width for the conductor length.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A metal wheel consists of an axle A, eight spokes and a rim as shown.

[A circular rim is joined by eight equally spaced radial spokes to the central axle A. One spoke and the rim are labelled.]

The rim has a radius of $0.65\ \mathrm{m}$ and the wheel rotates with an angular speed of $120\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. There is a uniform magnetic field of flux density $0.23\ \mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to the plane of the page.

What is the magnitude of the e.m.f. induced across each spoke?

A. $2.9\ \mathrm{V}$
B. $5.8\ \mathrm{V}$
C. $12\ \mathrm{V}$
D. $18\ \mathrm{V}$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A metal wheel consists of an axle A, eight spokes and a rim as shown. The rim has a radius of 0.65 m and the wheel rotates with an angular speed of −1 120 rad s

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must recognise the rotating spoke as sweeping out flux at a constant rate and relate the rotation period to angular speed.
questions.misconception: Using rim speed as the speed of the entire spoke

explanation.body: In one rotation, the spoke sweeps an area $A=\pi r^2$, so the flux swept is $BA$. The rotation period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, so the induced e.m.f. is $BA/T=\tfrac12 Br^2\omega$. Substituting gives $\tfrac12(0.23)(0.65)^2(120)=5.8\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Halving the flux rate again gives half the e.m.f. across one spoke.
perOption.B: Correct. The spoke sweeps flux at a rate of $5.8\ \mathrm{Wb\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Uses the rim speed along the whole spoke, giving twice the correct e.m.f.
perOption.D: Uses $B\omega r$, omitting the additional length and the factor of one-half from the swept-area calculation.

questions.stem:
A circular coil of 5 turns and radius 6.0 cm lies in the plane of the paper. A magnetic field acts perpendicularly into the paper as shown.

The magnetic flux density of the magnetic field changes in magnitude from 0.75 T to 0.18 T in 0.42 s.

What is the average e.m.f. induced in the coil?
questions.stemText: A circular coil of 5 turns and radius 6.0 cm lies in the plane of the paper. A magnetic field acts perpendicularly into the paper as shown. x x x x x x magnetic field into plane of paper x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x coil of 5 turns x x x x x x x x x x x x The magnetic flux density of the magnetic field changes in magnitude from 0.75 T to 0.18 T in 0.42 s. What is the average e.m.f. induced in the coil? A 15 mV B 72 mV C 77 mV D 96 mV

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of Faraday's law with flux linkage $NBA$.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the number of turns or using diameter/final B only

explanation.body: Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of the average induced e.m.f. as $\mathcal{E}=NA|\Delta B|/\Delta t$. Substitution gives $\mathcal{E}=\frac{5\pi(0.060)^2}{0.42}(0.75-0.18)=0.0767\ \mathrm{V}$, or $77\ \mathrm{mV}$.

perOption.A: Calculates the e.m.f. for one turn.
perOption.B: Uses a flux-density change smaller than 0.57 T or an equivalent underestimate of the flux-linkage change.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the ratio of the flux-linkage change to the elapsed time.

What is the reading on the ammeter?
questions.stemText: A 100% efficient transformer is connected as shown to a sinusoidal a.c. supply. primary coil secondary coil 200 turns 1000 turns A output a.c. supply 100  80 V a.c. What is the reading on the ammeter? A 0.16 A B 0.80 A C 2.8 A D 4.0 A

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Find secondary current, then use the turns ratio for an ideal transformer.
questions.misconception: Inverting the current ratio of a transformer (current steps the opposite way to voltage)

explanation.body: The secondary current is $I_s=V_s/R=80/100=0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. For the ideal transformer, $I_p/I_s=N_s/N_p$, so $I_p=(1000/200)(0.80)=4.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the current ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the secondary current as the ammeter reading.
perOption.C: Divides by the peak-to-r.m.s. factor even though the given a.c. voltage is already r.m.s.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem:
In a region of uniform magnetic field, a metal rod falls vertically from rest and lands on a slope. It continues to roll down the slope and launches off the slope as shown in the diagram.

The diagram shows the positions of the rod at times $t_{P}$, $t_{Q}$ and $t_{R}$ respectively.

cross-sectional view of the rod

Which graph best shows the variation with time t of the e.m.f. induced in the rod, from the time it is released?
questions.stemText: In a region of uniform magnetic field, a metal rod falls vertically from rest and lands on a slope. It continues to roll down the slope and launches off the slope as shown in the diagram. The diagram shows the positions of the rod at times tP, tQ and tR respectively. tP region of uniform magnetic field cross-sectional view of the rod tQ tR Which graph best shows the variation with time t of the e.m.f. induced in the rod, from the time it is released? A $t_{P}$ $t_{Q}$ $t_{R}$ t B $t_{P}$ $t_{Q}$ $t_{R}$ t C  D
questions.difficultyReason: The student must follow the component of velocity perpendicular to the field through three stages.
questions.misconception: Using the total speed in the motional e.m.f. formula

explanation.body: The induced e.m.f. is $E=Blv$, where $v$ is the horizontal component of the rod’s velocity. From P to Q the rod moves parallel to the field and $E=0$. From Q to R the constant component of weight along the slope makes the horizontal speed increase at a constant rate, so $E$ rises linearly. After R the rod is in projectile motion with constant horizontal velocity, so $E$ stays constant while it is in the field.

perOption.A: This drops the e.m.f. to zero at launch even though the rod retains horizontal velocity in the field.
perOption.B: Correct. The e.m.f. follows the horizontal velocity through all three stages.
perOption.C: This continues the horizontal acceleration after launch, when gravity acts vertically.
perOption.D: This gives a nonzero e.m.f. during the fall parallel to the field.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An ideal transformer is used to step-up a 240 V a.c. power supply. The output is used to heat a $1000\ \Omega$ resistive load. The ratio of the primary turns to secondary turns is 1:5.

[The primary coil on the left is connected to the 240 V a.c. supply. The secondary coil on the right is connected across a $1000\ \Omega$ resistor.]

What is the current in the primary coil?

A 0.24 A
B 1.2 A
C 6.0 A
D 36.0 A

stemImage.alt: Question 26: An ideal transformer is used to step-up a 240 V a.c. power supply. The output is used to heat a 1000  resistive load. The ratio of the primary turns to seconda

questions.difficultyReason: The student must step up the voltage, calculate the load current, and apply the transformer current ratio.
questions.misconception: Confusing primary and secondary current

explanation.body: The voltage ratio gives $V_s/V_p=5/1$, so $V_s=5\times240=1200\ \mathrm{V}$. The secondary current is $I_s=1200/1000=1.2\ \mathrm{A}$. Since $I_p/I_s=5/1$, the primary current is $I_p=5\times1.2=6.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: This can result from reversing the current ratio or applying the primary voltage directly to the load.
perOption.B: This is the secondary current through the load.
perOption.C: Correct. The primary current is five times the secondary current.
perOption.D: This overstates the current multiplication, which is a factor of five applied to 1.2 A.

A long straight wire is in the plane of a flat coil. The straight wire carries a constant current I as shown and is moved at a constant speed u towards the flat coil.

Which statement describing the current in the flat coil is true?
questions.stemText: A long straight wire is in the plane of a flat coil. The straight wire carries a constant current I as shown and is moved at a constant speed u towards the flat coil. I u Which statement describing the current in the flat coil is true? A The current is increasing. B The current is decreasing. C The current is always constant. D The current always changes direction.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires linking the inverse-distance field to an increasing rate of flux change.
questions.misconception: Assuming constant wire speed implies constant induced current.

explanation.body: As the wire approaches the coil at constant speed, its field $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)$ grows at an increasing rate as $d$ shrinks. The flux linkage therefore changes faster, increasing the induced e.m.f. and hence the coil current.

perOption.A: Correct. The rate of change of flux linkage increases.
perOption.B: Assumes the flux linkage changes more slowly as the wire moves closer.
perOption.C: Assumes constant speed gives a constant rate of flux change despite the inverse-distance field.
perOption.D: Assumes a reversal even though the flux through the coil keeps increasing in the same direction.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires using the gradient of a distance–time graph to infer the motional e.m.f.
questions.misconception: Reading the distance itself as proportional to the e.m.f.

explanation.body: For perpendicular motion in a uniform magnetic field, the induced e.m.f. is $E=Blv$. With $B$ and $l$ fixed, $E$ is proportional to the speed, given by the gradient of the $s$–$t$ graph. The gradient is initially small and constant, then larger and constant, and finally falls to zero and stays there, as shown in C.

perOption.A: Shows a falling e.m.f. while the rod initially moves at a constant speed.
perOption.B: Follows the shape of the distance graph and leaves a nonzero e.m.f. after the rod stops.
perOption.C: Correct. The e.m.f. follows the gradient of the distance–time graph.
perOption.D: Shows the e.m.f. rising during deceleration and staying nonzero after the rod stops.

questions.difficultyReason: It requires tracking the rate of change of overlap area and the reversal of current at exit.
questions.misconception: Using the flux itself to predict the induced current.

explanation.body: Split the frame into its triangular front and rectangular rear. As the triangular section enters or leaves the field, the area crossing the boundary per unit time grows, so the magnitudes of the rate of flux change, induced e.m.f. and induced current all rise. While the rectangular section crosses, the rate of flux change and the induced current magnitude are constant. The current is zero while the frame is wholly inside and reverses for exit because the flux then decreases.

perOption.A: Shows a constant exit current first, although the triangular tip reaches the exit boundary first.
perOption.B: Gives entry and exit the same current direction despite opposite flux changes.
perOption.C: Treats the rectangular section as crossing first at both boundaries.
perOption.D: Correct. Each crossing gives a ramp and a plateau, with opposite current directions.

In a similar set up, the South pole of the magnet is pushed into a coil of wire from end X at half the speed.

What is the maximum movement of the meter needle?

questions.misconception: Forgetting that reversing the pole reverses the induced current, or that the size depends on rate of change of flux

explanation.body: By Lenz's law the coil end X becomes a north pole when north approaches and a south pole when south approaches, reversing the current and the needle deflection. At half the speed, the flux linkage changes more slowly, so the induced e.m.f. and current are smaller.

perOption.A: Accounts for the smaller deflection but misses the reversal caused by switching poles.
perOption.B: Correct. The needle moves less than 10 units to the right.
perOption.C: Misses both the current reversal and the decrease in magnitude.
perOption.D: Gets the reversal right but treats slower insertion as producing a larger current.

questions.stemText:
A magnetic field of uniform flux density $0.045\ \mathrm{T}$ is at an angle of $60^\circ$ below the plane of horizontal coil of wire as shown.

[A horizontal circular coil is crossed by parallel magnetic field arrows pointing down and to the right. A dashed line in the coil’s plane makes a $60^\circ$ angle with the field lines.]

The coil of wire has 4 turns and cross sectional area of $0.30\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

What is the magnitude of the change in magnetic flux linkage of the coil of wire when it is flipped over $180^\circ$ about a horizontal axis?

A $0\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$; B $0.012\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$; C $0.035\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$; D $0.094\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A magnetic field of uniform flux density 0.045 T is at an angle of 60° below the plane of horizontal coil of wire as shown. The coil of wire has 4 turns and cro

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve the normal component of the field and account for the reversal of the area vector.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the sign reversal of flux linkage

explanation.body: The field component normal to the coil is $B\sin60^\circ$. Flipping the coil reverses the sign of the flux linkage, so the magnitude of the change is $NA[B\sin60^\circ-(-B\sin60^\circ)]$. Substituting gives $4(0.30)[0.045\sin60^\circ-(-0.045\sin60^\circ)]=0.094\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$.

perOption.A: Compares the magnitudes of the two linkages and misses the sign reversal.
perOption.B: $0.012\ \mathrm{Wb}$ is approximately the initial flux through one turn, before counting all four turns and the reversal.
perOption.C: Uses a change smaller than even the initial linkage magnitude of about $0.047\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The signed flux linkage reverses.

questions.stem:
A 20-turns square coil of side of length x = 8.0 mm is pivoted at its centre and placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density B = 0.010 T such that two sides of the coil are parallel to the field and two sides of the coil are perpendicular to the field as shown below. The coil rotates about the pivot with a frequency of 25 Hz.

What is the maximum e.m.f. induced by the coil?
questions.stemText: A 20-turns square coil of side of length x = 8.0 mm is pivoted at its centre and placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density B = 0.010 T such that two sides of the coil are parallel to the field and two sides of the coil are perpendicular to the field as shown below. The coil rotates about the pivot with a frequency of 25 Hz. coil x B pivot What is the maximum e.m.f. induced by the coil? A 1.3  $10^{-5}$ V B 3.2  $10^{-4}$ V C 2.0  $10^{-3}$ V D 1.2 V
questions.difficultyReason: The student must use the coil area, number of turns and angular speed to calculate the peak e.m.f.
questions.misconception: Confusing peak flux linkage with peak induced e.m.f.

explanation.body: The maximum induced e.m.f. is $E_0=NBA\omega=NBA(2\pi f)$. Substituting the coil area and frequency gives $(20)(0.010)(8.0\times10^{-3})^2[2\pi(25)]=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Gives the numerical value of the peak flux linkage before multiplying by angular speed.
perOption.B: Uses the frequency $f$ in place of $2\pi f$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the coil’s effective area or flux-change rate by hundreds of times.

The metal disc is rotated about an axis through its centre at 1500 revolutions per minute. An e.m.f. of $3.7\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{V}$ is induced between the centre of the metal disc and its rim.

[The circular metal disc rotates clockwise within a dashed rectangular region of uniform magnetic field of flux density $3.6\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$. Crosses indicate the field into the diagram. Separate contacts at the centre and at the bottom of the rim connect to terminals on the right.]

What is the area $A$ of the metal disc?

A. $2.2\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m^2}$
B. $4.1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$
C. $3.5\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$
D. $5.2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: The diagram below shows a metal disc of area A situated in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 3.6  10−5 T. The plane of the metal disc is perpendicular t

questions.difficultyReason: The unfamiliar disc geometry requires linking the area swept per turn to Faraday’s law and converting rpm to hertz.
questions.misconception: Treating the flux through the whole disc as the flux swept by a rotating radius

explanation.body: A radius sweeps area $A$ in one rotation of period $T$. Faraday’s law gives $E=|\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d}t|=BA/T=BAf$. Thus $3.7\times10^{-7}=(3.6\times10^{-5})A(1500/60)$, giving $A=4.1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

perOption.B: Correct.

[Diagram (a): flat coil with ends X and Y, vertical field lines passing through it, axis of rotation in the plane of the coil.] The coil is rotated around the axis and the induced e.m.f. E between X and Y varies with time t as shown in diagram (b). [Diagram (b): sinusoidal E–t graph starting at zero, peaks $\pm E_0$, about two cycles.] $E_0$ is the magnitude of the maximum induced e.m.f. Which diagram best represents how E varies with t if the frequency of rotation is doubled and the magnetic flux density remains the same? The dotted line shows the graph in diagram (b) for comparison. [A: same frequency, larger amplitude. B: double frequency, smaller amplitude. C: double frequency, same amplitude. D: double frequency, double amplitude.]

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A coil with N turns is placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density. The area of the coil is initially perpendicular to the field, as shown in diagram (a)

questions.difficultyReason: Needs E0 = NBAω so doubling frequency doubles both peak e.m.f. and frequency.
questions.misconception: Thinking only the frequency changes and the peak e.m.f. stays the same

explanation.body: The flux linkage is $NBA\cos(\omega t)$. Taking its negative time derivative gives $E=2\pi NBAf\sin(2\pi ft)$. Doubling $f$ doubles the peak e.m.f. to $2(2\pi NBAf)$ and halves the period.

perOption.A: Doubles the peak e.m.f. but keeps the original period.
perOption.B: Halves the period but incorrectly reduces the peak e.m.f.
perOption.C: Halves the period but keeps the original peak e.m.f.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A 120 turn coil of area 5.0 × $10^{-4}$ $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ is placed in a magnetic field of strength 5.0 × $10^{-2}$ T. The magnetic flux density B is then varied as shown.

What is the induced electromotive force when t = 3 s?
questions.stemText: A 120 turn coil of area 5.0 × 10–4 m2 is placed in a magnetic field of strength 5.0 × 10–2 T. The magnetic flux density B is then varied as shown. What is the induced electromotive force when t = 3 s? A 6.25 μV B 600 μV C 750 μV D 1250 μV
questions.difficultyReason: The student must read the slope on the falling segment and multiply by the coil area and turns.
questions.misconception: Using the average field change from the start of the graph.

explanation.body: At $t=3\ \mathrm{s}$, the graph is on the straight falling segment, so $|\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}t|=(5.0\times10^{-2})/(5-1)\ \mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}$. Taking the field perpendicular to the coil, Faraday’s law gives $|\mathcal{E}|=NA|\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}t|=120(5.0\times10^{-4})(5.0\times10^{-2})/4=750\ \mathrm{\mu V}$.

perOption.A: This is the induced e.m.f. per turn, leaving out the factor of 120.
perOption.B: This uses the average slope over all 5 seconds, including the flat segment.
perOption.C: Correct. It uses the local slope and all 120 turns.
perOption.D: This exceeds the e.m.f. given by the falling segment’s slope and the coil’s flux linkage.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows an iron-cored transformer assumed to be 100% efficient. The primary coil of the transformer has 4000 turns and is connected to a 240 V r.m.s. supply. The secondary coil has 200 turns and is connected, through an ideal diode, to a resistive load which is dissipating energy at a mean rate of 90 W.

What is the r.m.s. current in the secondary coil.
questions.stemText: The diagram shows an iron-cored transformer assumed to be 100% efficient. The primary coil of the transformer has 4000 turns and is connected to a 240 V r.m.s. supply. The secondary coil has 200 turns and is connected, through an ideal diode, to a resistive load which is dissipating energy at a mean rate of 90 W. primary secondary 90 W 240 V r.m.s. coil coil load 4000 turns 200 turns 4000 turns 200 turns What is the r.m.s. current in the secondary coil. A 0.375 A B 0.750 A C 7.50 A D 10.6 A
questions.difficultyReason: The student must account for both the transformer turns ratio and half-wave rectification before finding the r.m.s. current.
questions.misconception: Applying the unrectified secondary voltage directly across the load.

explanation.body: The secondary r.m.s. voltage is $(200/4000)(240)=12\ \mathrm{V}$. The diode removes one half-cycle, so the unrectified mean power would be $2(90)=180\ \mathrm{W}$ and $12^2/R=180$, giving $R=0.80\ \Omega$. With the diode in place, $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2(0.80)=90$, giving $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=10.6\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Dividing by the primary voltage uses the wrong side of the transformer and ignores rectification.
perOption.B: Doubling the load power and dividing by the primary voltage still does not give the secondary current.
perOption.C: Dividing 90 W by 12 V treats the full-wave secondary voltage as the r.m.s. load voltage.
perOption.D: Correct. This uses the mean power of the half-wave current.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A rectangular coil made of 100 turns of wire with cross sectional area $30\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ is placed within a uniform magnetic field of $0.80\ \mathrm{T}$. The coil is rotated with an angular velocity of $100\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. At different stages of its rotation, the cross sectional area of the coil can be parallel or perpendicular to the magnetic field, as shown.

[Two diagrams show a rectangular coil rotating about a dashed axis between pole pieces marked N on the left and S on the right. The coil plane is parallel to the magnetic field in the first diagram and perpendicular to it in the second.]

What is the maximum e.m.f. induced and the corresponding orientation of the coil?

A $0.24\ \mathrm{V}$, parallel to magnetic field
B $0.24\ \mathrm{V}$, perpendicular to magnetic field
C $24\ \mathrm{V}$, parallel to magnetic field
D $24\ \mathrm{V}$, perpendicular to magnetic field

stemImage.alt: Question 25: A rectangular coil made of 100 turns of wire with cross sectional area 30 cm2 is placed within a uniform magnetic field of 0.80 T. The coil is rotated with an a

questions.difficultyReason: Requires differentiating flux linkage and connecting the maximum slope to the coil orientation.
questions.misconception: Equating maximum flux linkage with maximum induced e.m.f.

explanation.body: The flux linkage is $NBA\sin(\omega t)$, so the e.m.f. has magnitude $\lvert\omega NBA\cos(\omega t)\rvert$. Its maximum is $\omega NBA=(100)(100)(0.80)[30(10^{-2})^2]=24\ \mathrm{V}$. The flux linkage changes fastest when it is zero, with the plane of the coil parallel to the field.

perOption.A: Omitting $\omega$ gives $0.24$, although the orientation is correct.
perOption.B: This omits $\omega$ and chooses the orientation where flux linkage is at an extremum.
perOption.C: Correct. The flux linkage changes fastest with the coil parallel to the field.
perOption.D: The magnitude is correct, but the e.m.f. is zero when the coil is perpendicular to the field.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An ideal transformer steps down the $240\ \mathrm{V}$ sinusoidal voltage from the mains to $12\ \mathrm{V}$, which is then applied to a variable load.

[The left side of a block labelled transformer is connected to the $240\ \mathrm{V}$ mains, and the right side is connected to a variable load shown as a variable resistor.]

What is the change in the current supplied by the mains when the resistance of the load is increased from $20\ \Omega$ to $50\ \Omega$?

A Decrease from $30\ \mathrm{mA}$ to $12\ \mathrm{mA}$.
B Increase from $12\ \mathrm{mA}$ to $30\ \mathrm{mA}$.
C Decrease from $12\ \mathrm{mA}$ to $4.8\ \mathrm{mA}$.
D Increase from $0.24\ \mathrm{A}$ to $0.60\ \mathrm{A}$.

stemImage.alt: Question 27: An ideal transformer steps down the 240 V sinusoidal voltage from the mains to 12 V, which is then applied to a variable load. 240 V mains variable load transfo

questions.difficultyReason: Requires calculating current on the load side at two resistances and converting to mains current.
questions.misconception: Confusing secondary current with mains current

explanation.body: For the ideal transformer, $I_\mathrm{p}/I_\mathrm{s}=N_\mathrm{s}/N_\mathrm{p}=V_\mathrm{s}/V_\mathrm{p}=12/240=0.050$. At $20\ \Omega$, $I_\mathrm{s}=12/20=0.60\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_\mathrm{p}=0.030\ \mathrm{A}$. At $50\ \Omega$, $I_\mathrm{s}=12/50=0.24\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_\mathrm{p}=0.012\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The mains current decreases from 30 mA to 12 mA.
perOption.B: This reverses the currents for the two load resistances.
perOption.C: This gives the correct final current as the starting value and scales it down again by $20/50$.
perOption.D: This uses the secondary currents and reverses their order.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A copper disc rotates with a constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field applied perpendicular to its surface, as shown. The axle and the edge of the disc are in contact with metallic brushes M and N which are connected to a resistor R via wires.

Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemText: A copper disc rotates with a constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field applied perpendicular to its surface, as shown. The axle and the edge of the disc are in contact with metallic brushes M and N which are connected to a resistor R via wires. resistor, R copper disc M N magnetic field into the plane direction of rotation Which of the following statements is correct? A There is no current through R because there is no flux change through the disc. B There is an alternating current through R. C There is a steady current from M, through R, to N. D There is a steady current from N, through R, to M.

options.label: A
options.text: There is no current through R because there is no flux change through the disc.

options.label: B
options.text: There is an alternating current through R.

options.label: C
options.text: There is a steady current from M, through R, to N.

options.label: D
options.text: There is a steady current from N, through R, to M.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer the induced current along a moving radius and trace its return path through the resistor.
questions.misconception: Applying the flux through the whole disc to the moving radius

explanation.body: Consider the radius from M to N, which is moving downwards at N as the disc rotates clockwise. By Lenz’s law the magnetic force opposes that motion, so it points upwards. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives conventional current from M to N within the disc, so a steady current returns from N through $R$ to M.

perOption.A: Uses the constant flux through the entire disc and misses the motional e.m.f. along its radius.
perOption.B: Assumes the e.m.f. reverses even though the rotation and magnetic field keep the same direction.
perOption.C: Uses the current direction inside the disc for the external return path.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A 240 V supply is connected to an ideal transformer. The output of the transformer is connected to five 12 V, 24 W lamps connected in parallel. The lamps are operating normally.

What is the current drawn from the supply?
questions.stemText: A 240 V supply is connected to an ideal transformer. The output of the transformer is connected to five 12 V, 24 W lamps connected in parallel. The lamps are operating normally. What is the current drawn from the supply? A 0.10 A B 0.50 A C 2.0 A D 10.0 A
questions.difficultyReason: Find the lamp current, add the parallel currents, then apply ideal transformer power balance.
questions.misconception: Confusing primary and secondary current

explanation.body: Each lamp draws $24/12=2.0\ \mathrm{A}$. The five lamps are in parallel, so the secondary current is $I_s=5(2.0)=10\ \mathrm{A}$. For an ideal transformer, $V_sI_s=V_pI_p$, so $12(10)=240I_p$ and $I_p=0.50\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Uses the power of just one lamp to calculate the supply current.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the current through a single lamp.
perOption.D: Gives the total secondary current.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
As a rectangular coil of dimensions L by H enters a magnetic field of flux density B at right angles with a constant speed v as shown in the figure below, an e.m.f. E is induced in the coil.

Which of the following will not increase the magnitude of E?
questions.stemText: As a rectangular coil of dimensions L by H enters a magnetic field of flux density B at right angles with a constant speed v as shown in the figure below, an e.m.f. E is induced in the coil. L magnetic field B H v Which of the following will not increase the magnitude of E? A Increase L B Increase H C Increase v D Increase B
questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying which coil dimension controls how fast the area inside the field changes.
questions.misconception: Confusing total flux change with its rate of change

explanation.body: The induced e.m.f. equals the rate of increase of flux linkage while the coil enters the field. The area inside the field increases at rate $Hv$, so $E=BHv$.

perOption.A: Correct. Increasing $L$ extends the entry time.
perOption.B: Increasing $H$ increases the area entering the field per second.
perOption.C: Increasing $v$ increases the area entering the field per second.
perOption.D: Increasing $B$ increases the flux through each unit of area.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A flat circular coil of 120 turns, each of area 0.070 $\mathrm{m}^{2}$, is placed with its axis parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The flux density of the field is changed steadily from 80 mT to 20 mT over a period of 4.0 s.

What is the e.m.f. induced in the coil during this time?
questions.stemText: A flat circular coil of 120 turns, each of area 0.070 m2, is placed with its axis parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The flux density of the field is changed steadily from 80 mT to 20 mT over a period of 4.0 s. What is the e.m.f. induced in the coil during this time? A 0 mV B 1.1 mV C 130 mV D 500 mV
questions.difficultyReason: The student must determine the field orientation and divide the flux-linkage change by time.
questions.misconception: Using change in flux linkage without dividing by time.

explanation.body: The coil axis is parallel to the field, so the field is normal to the area enclosed by the coil. The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is $NA|\Delta B|/\Delta t=120(0.070)(80-20)\times10^{-3}/4.0=0.126\ \mathrm V\approx130\ \mathrm{mV}$.

perOption.A: Treats the coil's axis as if it lay in the coil's plane and assumes zero flux.
perOption.B: Calculates the induced e.m.f. for just one turn.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the change in flux linkage without dividing by the 4.0 s interval.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A bar magnet is freely suspended so that it hangs horizontally above a flat aluminium disc which is rotating in a horizontal plane, as shown in figure below.

The bar magnet will
questions.stemText: A bar magnet is freely suspended so that it hangs horizontally above a flat aluminium disc which is rotating in a horizontal plane, as shown in figure below. The bar magnet will A rotate in the opposite direction to the disc. B rotate in the same direction as the disc. C remain at rest. D oscillate to and fro in the horizontal plane.

options.label: A
options.text: rotate in the opposite direction to the disc.

options.label: B
options.text: rotate in the same direction as the disc.

options.label: D
options.text: oscillate to and fro in the horizontal plane.

questions.difficultyReason: Needs applying Lenz's law to eddy currents in an unfamiliar set-up.
questions.misconception: Expecting no interaction because aluminium is non-magnetic

explanation.body: By Lenz’s law, the eddy currents induced in the rotating disc oppose the change in magnetic flux through the disc. Their torque on the suspended magnet reduces the relative rotation, so the magnet turns in the same direction as the disc.

perOption.A: Opposite rotation would increase the relative motion driving the induction.
perOption.B: Correct. The induced torque drags the magnet in the disc’s direction.
perOption.C: Ignores the torque exerted by the induced currents.
perOption.D: Assumes a reversing torque even though the rotating disc initially drags the magnet in one direction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A generator produces a current of 60.0 A r.m.s at a voltage of 120 V r.m.s. An ideal transformer steps up the voltage to a peak value of 4500 V and transmits the power through a cable of total resistance 40.0 $\Omega$ to the consumers. What is the percentage of power transmitted to the consumers? A 94.3 % B 97.2 % C 98.6 % D 99.3 %

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A generator produces a current of 60.0 A r.m.s at a voltage of 120 V r.m.s. An ideal transformer steps up the voltage to a peak value of 4500 V and transmits th

questions.difficultyReason: Chains transformer power, peak-to-r.m.s. conversion and $I^2R$ loss.
questions.misconception: Using the peak voltage instead of the r.m.s. voltage

explanation.body: The mean input power is $120(60.0)=7200\ \mathrm{W}$. The ideal transformer supplies the same power at $4500/\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V}$ r.m.s., so the cable current is $I_{\rm rms}=7200\sqrt{2}/4500\ \mathrm{A}$. After the cable loss, the power delivered is $P'=7200-I_{\rm rms}^2(40.0)$. The percentage delivered is $(P'/7200)\times100\%\approx97.2\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the peak cable current in the mean power-loss formula and doubles the loss.
perOption.B: Correct. About 97.2% of the power reaches the consumers.
perOption.C: Treats 4500 V as the r.m.s. voltage, halving the calculated cable loss.
perOption.D: Converts peak voltage to r.m.s. in the wrong direction by multiplying by √2, leaving only a quarter of the correct cable loss.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An aluminium ring is suspended near one end of a long coil of wire and a magnet is placed near the other end with its north pole facing the coil as shown. Assume that the magnetic field from the magnet does not reach the ring.

[The ring hangs to the left of the coil and the bar magnet lies to the right, all on the same axis. The magnet's N pole is on the left and its S pole is on the right. A wire joins the coil terminals to form a closed circuit.]

Which of the following describes the motion of the ring when the magnet is first pushed towards the coil, and then pulled away?

Options (magnet pushed towards coil, magnet pulled away from coil)
A ring swings left, ring swings left
B ring swings right, ring swings left
C ring swings left, ring swings right
D ring swings right, ring swings right

stemImage.alt: Question 26: An aluminium ring is suspended near one end of a long coil of wire and a magnet is placed near the other end with its north pole facing the coil as shown. Assum

appearances.originalFile: grail:16186 2017 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must follow induction from the magnet to the coil and then from the coil to the ring in both cases.
questions.misconception: Reversing the coil current alone reverses the force on the ring.

explanation.body: Pushing the magnet towards the coil induces a current in the coil and builds up its magnetic field through the ring. By Faraday’s and Lenz’s laws, the ring’s induced current opposes that buildup, so the coil repels it to the left. When the magnet is pulled away, the coil’s field builds up in the opposite direction, so the ring’s current also reverses and the ring is again repelled to the left.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Predicts attraction on approach even though the ring opposes the buildup of the coil’s field.
perOption.C: Predicts attraction on withdrawal even though the coil’s field builds up in the opposite direction and the ring’s current reverses too.
perOption.D: Predicts attraction in both cases even though the ring initially opposes the buildup of the coil’s field in each case.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The magnetic flux linking a conducting loop changes sinusoidally with time.

Which of the following describes the phase difference between the magnetic flux linkage and the e.m.f. induced?

A They are in phase with each other.
B They are out of phase by $\pi/4\ \mathrm{rad}$.
C They are out of phase by $\pi/2\ \mathrm{rad}$.
D They are out of phase by $\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$.

stemImage.alt: Question 27: The magnetic flux linking a conducting loop changes sinusoidally with time. Which of the following describes the phase difference between the magnetic flux link

appearances.originalFile: grail:16186 2017 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student links Faraday’s law to the quarter-cycle shift between sine and cosine.
questions.misconception: The minus sign in Faraday’s law gives a half-cycle shift relative to the flux.

explanation.body: By Faraday’s law, the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the negative time derivative of the flux linkage. A sinusoidal flux linkage therefore gives a cosine e.m.f. up to a sign, so the phase difference is $\pi/2\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Treats the e.m.f. as proportional to the flux linkage itself.
perOption.B: Uses an eighth-cycle shift where differentiation gives a quarter-cycle shift.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the minus sign alone and omits the phase shift from differentiation.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The primary coil of a transformer is connected to an alternating voltage supply. The secondary coil is connected across a variable resistor.

Which change will cause an increase in the p.d. across the secondary coil?
questions.stemText: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to an alternating voltage supply. The secondary coil is connected across a variable resistor. 6.5 mV R primary coil secondary coil primary coil secondary coil Which change will cause an increase in the p.d. across the secondary coil? A decreasing the cross-sectional area of the secondary coil B decreasing the current in the primary coil C decreasing the resistance of the variable resistor D decreasing the number of turns of the primary coil

options.label: A
options.text: decreasing the cross-sectional area of the secondary coil

options.label: B
options.text: decreasing the current in the primary coil

options.label: C
options.text: decreasing the resistance of the variable resistor

options.label: D
options.text: decreasing the number of turns of the primary coil

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Applies the ideal transformer turns ratio at fixed input voltage.
questions.misconception: Treating load resistance as a control for ideal secondary voltage

explanation.body: For an ideal transformer, $V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p$. With $V_p$ and $N_s$ fixed, decreasing $N_p$ increases $V_s$.

perOption.A: Under the key's flux model, reducing the coil area reduces the induced e.m.f. $E=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$.
perOption.B: With $V_p$ and $I_s$ fixed, decreasing $I_p$ would decrease $V_s$ by $V_s/V_p=I_p/I_s$.
perOption.C: A smaller load resistance changes the secondary current while the ideal secondary voltage stays fixed.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
In the circuit shown below, the switch is initially open and the variable resistor is set to its maximum resistance. The switch is closed quickly.

The resistance of the variable resistor is then gradually decreased to its minimum value, after which the switch is opened quickly.

At which stage is the magnitude of the current through the ammeter greatest?
questions.stemText: In the circuit shown below, the switch is initially open and the variable resistor is set to its maximum resistance. The switch is closed quickly. The resistance of the variable resistor is then gradually decreased to its minimum value, after which the switch is opened quickly. soft iron A At which stage is the magnitude of the current through the ammeter greatest? A immediately after the switch is closed B while the resistance is being decreased C when the resistance reaches its minimum value D immediately after the switch is opened

options.label: A
options.text: immediately after the switch is closed

options.label: B
options.text: while the resistance is being decreased

options.label: C
options.text: when the resistance reaches its minimum value

options.label: D
options.text: immediately after the switch is opened

questions.difficultyReason: Compare how fast the flux changes at each stage in the two-coil circuit.
questions.misconception: Equating the largest primary current with the largest induced current

explanation.body: The primary current is greatest just before the switch opens, when the variable resistance is at its minimum. Opening the switch quickly then causes the greatest rate of change of magnetic flux through the soft iron. This gives the largest induced e.m.f. and hence the largest current through the ammeter.

perOption.A: The switch closes with the resistance at its maximum, so the change in primary current is smaller.
perOption.B: The gradual resistance change changes the flux more slowly.
perOption.C: Minimum resistance gives the largest steady primary current, but the secondary current depends on how fast the flux is changing.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A circular coil of area $300\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.0500\ \mathrm T$. The coil has 50 turns and a resistance of $10.0\ \Omega$. It is connected to a circuit with a galvanometer with the circuit resistance also being $10.0\ \Omega$.

What is the quantity of charge that flows when the coil is suddenly removed out of the magnetic field?

A  $7.50\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm C$
B  $3.75\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm C$
C  $7.50\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm C$
D  $3.75\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm C$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A circular coil of area 300 cm2 is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.0500 T. The coil has 50 turns and a resistance of 10.0 Ω

questions.difficultyReason: Combine Faraday’s law with the current–charge relation and include both resistances.
questions.misconception: Using only the coil resistance or mis-converting square centimetres

explanation.body: Faraday’s law gives $\mathcal E=-\mathrm d(NBA)/\mathrm dt$. Using $\mathcal E=RI$ and $I=\mathrm dQ/\mathrm dt$ gives $R\,\mathrm dQ/\mathrm dt=-\mathrm d(NBA)/\mathrm dt$. The flux drops to zero, so the charge magnitude is $\Delta Q=NBA/R=\frac{50}{10+10}(0.0500)(300\times10^{-4})=3.75\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm C$.

perOption.A: This omits the circuit’s additional resistance and makes the converted area 100 times too small.
perOption.B: This makes the converted area 100 times too small.
perOption.C: This includes only one of the two $10.0\ \Omega$ resistances.
perOption.D: Correct.

In which coil does the magnitude of the magnetic flux density have the greatest variation?

[The ring has a 2-turn coil A at the wider lower-left section, a 3-turn coil B on the left connected to an a.c. supply, a 4-turn coil C at the narrowest section at the top, and a 5-turn coil D on the right.]

questions.misconception: Confusing flux density with flux linkage

explanation.body: The same magnetic flux $\Phi$ passes through the soft-iron ring at all four coils. Since $\Phi=BA$, the variation in $B$ is greatest where the core area is smallest, at C. The number of turns affects the induced emf through flux linkage.

perOption.A: The wider core at A gives a smaller variation in flux density.
perOption.B: Being connected to the supply does not give B the smallest core area.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The extra turn affects flux linkage, while D has a larger core area than C.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The root mean square (rms) current in the primary coil of an ideal transformer is $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$. The rms voltage in the secondary coil is $50\ \mathrm{V}$. The average power transferred from the secondary coil is $20\ \mathrm{W}$.

What is $N_{\mathrm p}/N_{\mathrm s}$ and what is the average power transferred from the primary coil?

$N_{\mathrm p}/N_{\mathrm s}$ | Average power transferred from the primary coil / W
A $1/5$ | $4.0$
B $5$ | $20$
C $1/5$ | $20$
D $5$ | $100$

questions.difficultyReason: It combines power conservation, rms values and the transformer voltage ratio.
questions.misconception: Inverting the primary-to-secondary turns ratio

explanation.body: The ideal transformer has no power loss, so the primary transfers $20\ \mathrm{W}$. With the assumed unity power factor, $P_{\mathrm p}=V_{\mathrm p}I_{\mathrm p}$ gives $20=V_{\mathrm p}(2.0)$ and $V_{\mathrm p}=10\ \mathrm{V}$. The turns ratio is $N_{\mathrm p}/N_{\mathrm s}=V_{\mathrm p}/V_{\mathrm s}=10/50=1/5$.

perOption.A: Scales the power by the turns ratio, despite power conservation.
perOption.B: Inverts the turns ratio obtained under the unity-power-factor assumption.
perOption.C: Correct under the unity-power-factor assumption.
perOption.D: Uses the secondary voltage with the primary current and overstates the transmitted power.

A magnetic field of flux density $4.0\times10^{-4}$ T passes through a coil of wire of 50 turns and an area of 30 cm$^2$. The field makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal plane of the coil. [Diagram: field lines crossing the horizontal coil at 60° to its plane; horizontal axis shown.]

What is the e.m.f. induced in the coil when it is turned over once about its horizontal axis in a time of 0.60 s?
A $5.0\times10^{-5}$ V
B $8.7\times10^{-5}$ V
C $1.0\times10^{-4}$ V
D $1.7\times10^{-4}$ V

stemImage.alt: Question 25: A magnetic field of flux density 4.0 10−  4 T passes through a coil of wire of 50 turns and an area of 30 cm2. The field makes an angle of 60° with the horizon

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the angle to the plane (sin not cos) and the factor 2 for flipping the coil.
questions.misconception: Uses $\cos60^\circ$ instead of $\sin60^\circ$, or forgets the factor 2 from flipping.

explanation.body:
Turning the coil over once reverses the flux through it, so the change in flux linkage is $2NBA\sin60^\circ$.

$\varepsilon = \dfrac{(2)(50)(30\times10^{-4})(4.0\times10^{-4})\sin60^\circ}{0.60}$

$= 1.7\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{V}$

perOption.A: Uses $\cos60^\circ$ and no factor of 2: $NBA\cos60^\circ/t = 5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.B: Omits the factor of 2 for turning the coil over.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos60^\circ$ with the factor of 2, taking the angle from the normal.
perOption.D: Correct. $2NBA\sin60^\circ/t$.

The induced current in the inner loop is

The current in the outer loop is clockwise and changes with time as shown in Fig. 26 (b). current inner loop outer loop time Fig. 26 (a) Fig. 26 (b) The induced current in the inner loop is A constant in the clockwise direction. B variable in the clockwise direction. C constant in the anticlockwise direction. D variable in the anticlockwise direction.
questions.difficultyReason: Combines Lenz's law direction with a constant $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t$ giving constant e.m.f.
questions.misconception: Applies Lenz's law backwards, or thinks a changing current gives a changing e.m.f.

explanation.body:
The inner loop experiences a decreasing flux linkage, so by Lenz's law the induced current flows in the same direction as that in the outer loop (clockwise) to oppose the decrease.

The current in the outer loop decreases at a constant rate, so the rate of decrease of $B$ and hence of flux linkage is constant. The induced e.m.f. in the inner loop is therefore constant, and so is the induced current.

perOption.A: Correct. Constant and clockwise.
perOption.B: Direction is right, but the rate of change of flux is constant so the current is not variable.
perOption.C: Direction is opposite to what Lenz's law requires for a decreasing flux.
perOption.D: Both direction and constancy are wrong.

The direction of the current alternates between clockwise and anticlockwise depending on which radius is cutting the flux (use Fleming's right-hand rule), giving a square wave.

perOption.B: Triangular waveform would need a changing rate of flux cutting.

questions.stemText: The diagram shows a coil placed in a uniform magnetic field. In the position shown, the angle between the normal to the plane of the coil and the magnetic field is $\frac{\pi}{3}$ rad. [Diagram: horizontal uniform field lines pointing right; a coil on a vertical axle drawn edge-on, tilted, with its normal at $\pi/3$ to the field; arrows show clockwise and anticlockwise rotation directions.] Which row shows the angles through which the coil should be rotated, and the direction of rotation, so that the flux linkage and the induced e.m.f. becomes a maximum? A flux linkage: $\pi/6$ clockwise; e.m.f.: $\pi/3$ anticlockwise. B flux linkage: $\pi/6$ anticlockwise; e.m.f.: $\pi/3$ clockwise. C flux linkage: $\pi/3$ clockwise; e.m.f.: $\pi/6$ anticlockwise. D flux linkage: $\pi/3$ anticlockwise; e.m.f.: $\pi/6$ clockwise.

stemImage.alt: Question 25: The diagram shows a coil placed in a uniform magnetic field. In the position shown, the angle between the normal to the plane of the coil and the magnetic field

questions.difficultyReason: Needs a spatial picture of coil, normal and field, and the fact that flux linkage and e.m.f. are out of phase.
questions.misconception: Thinking e.m.f. is maximum when flux linkage is maximum.

explanation.body:
Maximum flux linkage occurs when the B field lines are perpendicular to the coil, i.e. the normal is parallel to the field. This needs a rotation of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ anticlockwise.

When flux linkage is maximum, the induced e.m.f. is minimum (zero), and vice-versa. So the e.m.f. is maximum when the coil plane is parallel to the field, a further $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ away from that position, i.e. a rotation of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ clockwise from the initial position.

perOption.A: Rotation angles and directions are both reversed between the two cases.
perOption.B: The directions are right for neither case: the flux-linkage rotation should be $\pi/3$, not $\pi/6$.
perOption.C: Angles are swapped between the two cases and the directions are wrong.
perOption.D: Correct. $\pi/3$ anticlockwise for maximum flux linkage, $\pi/6$ clockwise for maximum e.m.f.

questions.stemText: The primary coil of a step-up ideal transformer is connected to a source of alternating p.d. The secondary coil is connected to a lamp. [Diagram: a.c. source connected to the primary coil, an iron core, and a secondary coil connected to a lamp.] Which row correctly describes the ratios of flux linkages and currents through the secondary coil in relation to the primary coil? Columns: (secondary flux linkage)/(primary flux linkage) and (secondary current)/(primary current). A <1, <1; B >1, <1; C >1, >1; D <1, >1.

stemImage.alt: Question 26: The primary coil of a step-up ideal transformer is connected to a source of alternating p.d. The secondary coil is connected to a lamp. Which row correctly desc

questions.difficultyReason: Needs to separate flux (same in both coils) from flux linkage (N times flux) and apply the ideal-transformer current ratio.
questions.misconception: Believing the flux linkage is the same in primary and secondary coils.

explanation.body:
A step-up transformer has $N_s > N_p$.

For an ideal transformer the magnetic flux $\phi$ through each turn is the same in both coils, so flux linkage is $N_s\phi > N_p\phi$, giving a ratio $>1$.

$\dfrac{I_s}{I_p} = \dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s} < 1$.

perOption.A: Flux linkage ratio is $N_s/N_p > 1$, not less than 1.
perOption.B: Correct. Flux linkage ratio $>1$, current ratio $<1$.
perOption.C: The current ratio is less than 1, since power is conserved and the secondary voltage is larger.
perOption.D: Both ratios are reversed.

questions.stem:
An aluminium disc of diameter d rotates about its centre. A point on the rim moves at a constant speed v. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to its surface. A steady electromotive force (e.m.f.) E is generated between the centre O and the rim at P.

What is the expression for the e.m.f E generated?

A steady electromotive force (e.m.f.) E is generated between the centre O and the rim at P. P d O v What is the expression for the e.m.f E generated? A Bdv B 4 Bdv C 2 D Bdv Bv

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must relate rim speed to rotation frequency and then to the flux swept per unit time.
questions.misconception: Every point along the radius moves at the rim speed.

explanation.body: At the rim, $v=r\omega=2\pi fr$, so $f=v/(2\pi r)$. A radius sweeps an area $\pi r^2$ per revolution, giving $E=B\pi r^2f$. Substituting gives $E=Brv/2=Bdv/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the entire radius as moving at the rim speed, giving $B(d/2)v$.
perOption.C: Uses the full diameter with the rim speed in the straight-conductor expression.
perOption.D: Omits a length factor, so the expression does not have units of voltage.

A $\dfrac{N_p^2 V_p}{N_s^2 R}$
B $\dfrac{N_s V_p^2}{N_p R}$
C $\dfrac{N_s^2 V_p^2}{N_p^2 R}$

questions.difficultyReason: Two standard relations (turns ratio and $V^2/R$) combined algebraically.
questions.misconception: squaring only part of the expression for $V_s$

explanation.body:
For an ideal transformer, $V_s = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}V_p$.

Power in the secondary $= \dfrac{V_s^2}{R} = \dfrac{(N_s V_p/N_p)^2}{R} = \dfrac{N_s^2 V_p^2}{N_p^2 R}$, and since the transformer is ideal this equals the power in the primary coil.

A rectangular coil moves in a direction parallel to a long straight current-carrying conductor as shown below.

The conductor carries a steady direct current. Which of the following statements is true?
questions.stemText: A rectangular coil moves in a direction parallel to a long straight current-carrying conductor as shown below. rectangular coil long conductor with steady direct current The conductor carries a steady direct current. Which of the following statements is true? A There is no induced current in the coil. B The induced current flows clockwise in the coil. C The magnitude of the induced current in the coil is proportional to 1 . 2 D The magnitude of the induced current in the coil varies with the speed at which the coil is moving.
questions.difficultyReason: Recognising that the field is uniform along the direction of motion gives the answer quickly.
questions.misconception: Thinking any motion of a coil in a magnetic field induces a current

explanation.body:
As the coil moves parallel to the conductor, its distance from the wire does not change, so the magnetic flux linking it stays constant.

The rate of change of magnetic flux linkage is zero, so the induced e.m.f. is zero and there is no induced current.

perOption.A: Correct. The flux linkage does not change, so no e.m.f. is induced.
perOption.B: There is no induced current at all, so it has no direction.
perOption.C: There is no induced current, so its magnitude cannot depend on anything.
perOption.D: Moving faster parallel to the wire still gives no change in flux, so the current stays zero.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An aluminium disc is rotated about its centre O at a constant angular speed. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its surface. X and Z are on the circumference, and Y is midway between O and X. The magnitude of the e.m.f. between any two points, for instance “X” and “Y”, is denoted as $E_{\mathrm{XY}}$.

Which of the following options is correct?
questions.stemText: An aluminium disc is rotated about its centre O at a constant angular speed. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its surface. X and Z are on the circumference, and Y is midway between O and X. The magnitude of the e.m.f. between any two points, for instance “X” and “Y”, is denoted as EXY. Y O X Z Which of the following options is correct? A $E_{\mathrm{XY}}$ < $E_{YO}$ B $E_{XY}$ = $E_{YO}$ C $E_{XY}$ < $E_{YZ}$ D $E_{XY}$ = $E_{YZ}$
questions.difficultyReason: Requires reasoning about potential distribution in a rotating disc, an unfamiliar context.
questions.misconception: Assuming equal lengths of the disc give equal induced e.m.f.s

explanation.body:
Electrons accumulate either at the centre or at the rim. In either case, two points equidistant from O have the same potential, and the potential difference between O and a point gets larger with distance from O. Y and X are on the same line from O, and Z is at the same radius as X, so $E_{XY} = E_{YZ}$.

Points further from O travel faster, so the segment XY cuts flux faster than YO. Therefore $E_{XY} > E_{YO}$.

perOption.A: Section XY moves faster than YO and cuts flux faster, so $E_{XY} > E_{YO}$.
perOption.B: Points further from O move faster, so equal lengths XY and YO do not give equal e.m.f.s.
perOption.C: X and Z are at the same radius and hence the same potential, so $E_{YZ} = E_{XY}$.
perOption.D: Correct. X and Z are equidistant from O, so they have the same potential.

questions.stemText:
A conducting rod of length $L$ is released from rest at the top of a smooth sloping surface. The surface has a fixed length $y$, but the angle $\theta$ of the slope to the horizontal can be varied. There is a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$ throughout the region of the sloping surface directed vertically downwards.

[Diagram: 3D view of a wedge with a horizontal rod lying across the slope, moving down the slope of length $y$ at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal; $B$ points vertically downwards. A side view shows the rod on the incline moving down the slope, with $B$ vertically downwards.]

Which value of $\theta$ will induce the largest e.m.f. in the rod when it reaches the bottom of the slope?

A $35^\circ$
B $40^\circ$
C $45^\circ$
D $50^\circ$

stemImage.alt: Question 23: A conducting rod of length L is released from rest at the top of a smooth sloping surface. The surface has a fixed length y, but the angle  of the slope to the

questions.difficultyReason: Combines kinematics on an incline with the perpendicular velocity component in the e.m.f., then compares a non-obvious trade-off.
questions.misconception: Using the full speed rather than the component perpendicular to the field

explanation.body:
The induced e.m.f. is $\varepsilon = BLv\cos\theta$, where $v$ is the rod's speed at the bottom of the slope (only the component of velocity perpendicular to the vertical field counts).

To find $v$: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 0 + 2(g\sin\theta)y$, so $v = \sqrt{2yg\sin\theta}$.

Hence $\varepsilon = BL\sqrt{2yg}\,\left(\sqrt{\sin\theta}\right)\cos\theta$.

Evaluating $\sqrt{\sin\theta}\cos\theta$: $35^\circ$ gives $0.620$, $40^\circ$ gives $0.614$, $45^\circ$ gives $0.595$, $50^\circ$ gives $0.563$. So $35^\circ$ gives the largest e.m.f.

perOption.A: Correct. $\sqrt{\sin\theta}\cos\theta = 0.620$ is the largest of the four.
perOption.B: $\sqrt{\sin 40^\circ}\cos 40^\circ = 0.614$, slightly smaller than at $35^\circ$.
perOption.C: $\sqrt{\sin 45^\circ}\cos 45^\circ = 0.595$; maximising $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ (forgetting the square root on speed) would wrongly favour $45^\circ$.
perOption.D: $\sqrt{\sin 50^\circ}\cos 50^\circ = 0.563$; a steeper slope gives more speed but a smaller perpendicular velocity component.

A increase the frequency of the alternating supply B decrease the cross-sectional area of coil P C decrease the number of turns in coil Q D insert an iron core through both coils

options.label: C

questions.difficultyReason: Requires keeping frequency fixed while increasing induced e.m.f., ruling out the tempting frequency change.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that changing supply frequency also changes the trace's frequency

explanation.body: Inserting an iron core concentrates the magnetic field lines and gives better flux linkage between coils P and Q. The flux linkage through both coils is larger, so the amplitude of the voltage induced in coil Q increases, while the frequency stays at 50 Hz.

perOption.A: Increasing the frequency raises the amplitude in Q (faster rate of change of flux linkage), but the number of cycles per unit time also increases.
perOption.B: According to the school, decreasing the cross-sectional area of coil P does not change the flux density it produces, so the flux linkage does not increase.
perOption.C: Fewer turns in Q gives a lower amplitude, since $V_Q/V_P = N_Q/N_P$.
perOption.D: Correct. The iron core increases the flux linkage without changing the frequency.

The following circuit was set up to test a transformer. The input a.c. voltage $V_p$ is 450 V, with a current $I_p$ of 4.0 mA. The number of turns in the secondary coil, $N_s$ is 240 with a current $I_s$ of 120 mA.

A zero
B $\dfrac{E}{4}$
C $\dfrac{E}{2}$
D $\dfrac{3E}{4}$

stemImage.alt: Question 25: An aluminium disc of radius r rotates about its centre at a constant speed. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its surface. A steady elec

questions.difficultyReason: Requires knowing the disc e.m.f. scales with r² and taking a difference between two radii.
questions.misconception: Assuming the disc e.m.f. is proportional to radius

explanation.body:
The e.m.f. between the centre O and a point at radius $r$ is $E = B\pi r^2 f$ (flux swept per revolution times revolutions per second).

Between O and Q, at radius $r/2$: $E_{OQ} = B\pi\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)^2 f = \dfrac{E}{4}$.

perOption.B: This is the e.m.f. between O and Q, not between Q and P.
perOption.C: Assumes e.m.f. is proportional to $r$; it is proportional to $r^2$ (area swept).
perOption.D: Correct. $E_{QP} = E - E/4 = 3E/4$.

explanation.body: By Faraday’s law, $\mathcal E=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(NBA\cos\omega t)=\omega NBA\sin\omega t$. The maximum is therefore $(2\pi f)NBA$. Using $f=1800/60\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $A=\pi(1.0\times10^{-2})^2/4\ \mathrm{m^2}$ gives $\mathcal E_{\max}=1.8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the peak rate of change of the total flux linkage.
perOption.B: Uses $f$ in place of $\omega=2\pi f$.
perOption.C: Correct. The peak emf is $\omega NBA$.
perOption.D: Overestimates the peak rate of change of the total flux linkage.

questions.difficultyReason: Needs Lenz's law applied to both the pole and the end being changed, plus Faraday's law for the size.
questions.misconception: Thinking that changing the pole always reverses the current, regardless of which end it enters

explanation.body:
At half the speed the rate of change of flux linkage halves, so the induced e.m.f. and current are smaller: less than 10 units.

Pushing a N pole into the left end makes the coil act as a magnet with N at that end. Pushing a S pole into the right end makes the right end S, which is the same N–S polarity of the coil. So the induced current is in the same direction and the needle again moves to the left.

perOption.A: Correct. Same current direction, smaller rate of flux change.
perOption.B: The direction does not reverse. Reversing the pole and the end together gives the same induced polarity in the coil.
perOption.C: Half the speed gives a smaller e.m.f., not a larger one.
perOption.D: Both the direction and the size are wrong: the deflection is to the left and smaller.

questions.difficultyReason: Combines the direction of force on moving charges with resolving the rod length perpendicular to the velocity.
questions.misconception: Using the full rod length instead of its component perpendicular to the velocity

explanation.body:
Using Fleming's left-hand rule, electrons in the conductor moving to the right experience an upward force in a magnetic field pointing out of the page. Electrons gather at R, so S is at the higher potential.

$\varepsilon = Blv = (2.8 \times 10^{-3})(15 \times 10^{-2} \times \sin 60^\circ)(10) = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V} = 3.6\ \mathrm{mV}$

Each quantity in the equation must be the components perpendicular to each other, so only the vertical length $l\sin 60^\circ$ counts.

perOption.A: Correct p.d., but the wrong end: the electrons are pushed towards R, making R negative.
perOption.B: Wrong end, and uses the full 15 cm length instead of its component perpendicular to the velocity.
perOption.C: Correct. Electrons collect at R, and $\varepsilon = B(l\sin 60^\circ)v = 3.6\ \mathrm{mV}$.
perOption.D: Correct end, but uses the full 15 cm length instead of the component perpendicular to the velocity.

explanation.body: Multiply the number of turns $N$ by the field component normal to the coil and by the coil area $A$. Since $\theta$ is the angle to the plane, this gives $N\times B\sin\theta\times A=BNA\sin\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses the component parallel to the plane and omits the number of turns.
perOption.B: Calculates only the flux through one turn.
